name: Epsilon Labs catalogue
pricing_note: Prices are not published. Every engagement is scoped and quoted after a call — er@epsilon-labs.co

offers.name: Pre-Fab Design Review
offers.tagline: Find the board-killer before you pay for a hundred of them.
offers.summary: Send us your schematic and BOM before you commit to fabrication. We review it the way we review our own and send back a written findings list, ranked by what it would cost you to discover later.
offers.price_drivers: Layer count and part count. A four-layer mixed-signal board with 300 components is not a two-layer sensor board, and we will tell you which you have before you pay.
deliverables: Written findings list, ranked by cost-if-missed
Power architecture review — rails, margin, protection, thermal
Voltage-domain check across every interface on the board
Footprint and land-pattern spot check against manufacturer datasheets
BOM review — lifecycle risk, lead times, second sources
DRC readiness and fabrication-output check
A call to walk through anything you want to argue about
for: You have a board about to go to fabrication and nobody senior has read it
A previous revision came back wrong and you do not know why
Your layout was outsourced and you want it checked before you pay the fab
You are a software team who inherited a hardware product
not_for: Boards already in production with no revision planned — there is nothing to act on
Full layout work. That is Board-to-Fab.
Certification, EMC pre-compliance or safety approval. We are not a test house.

offers.name: Protocol Decode Sprint
offers.tagline: Your machine is already talking. We work out what it is saying.
offers.summary: A serial bus with no published specification, no vendor support and no integration partner willing to return a call. We capture it, decode it, and hand you a validated parser plus the written specification nobody else has.
offers.price_drivers: How many genuinely distinct protocols there are, whether we can get physical access for the capture phase, and how much other traffic shares the bus. One vendor across several model years is almost always one protocol; separate vendors are separate sprints.
deliverables: Written protocol specification — framing, delimiters, field map, encoding, checksums
Validated parser in C/C++ or Python, with the capture set it was verified against
Raw captures and the stimulus matrix used to produce them, so you can re-derive it
Resynchronisation strategy for a shared or noisy bus
A go/no-go call at the halfway point — if it is no-go you stop there and we refund the balance
for: Fuel dispensers, industrial meters, weighbridges, PLCs, medical or lab instruments
RS485, RS232, Modbus, CAN, or something proprietary on top of one of them
A vendor who will not share the specification, or no longer exists
A mixed fleet where every machine speaks slightly differently
not_for: Encrypted or cryptographically authenticated protocols — that is a different problem and usually the wrong one to solve
Any equipment you do not own or have written authorisation from the owner to interface with. We ask in writing before we start, every time, and we will decline without it.
Wireless or network protocols. This is wires.

offers.name: Board-to-Fab
offers.tagline: Schematic to fabrication-ready, owned by you.
offers.summary: Schematic capture, PCB layout, custom symbol and footprint libraries drawn from datasheets, an orderable BOM and a complete fabrication package. Everything needed to build it again without us.
offers.price_drivers: Layer count, part count, mechanical and enclosure constraints, and whether firmware is in scope. Firmware alongside the board is cheaper than firmware after it, because the person who drew the board writes the driver.
deliverables: Schematic, in KiCad 9 and as a readable PDF
PCB layout, routed to clean DRC, with power on a widened netclass
Custom symbol and footprint libraries drawn from manufacturer datasheets
Orderable BOM with distributor part numbers and qualified alternates
Fabrication package — Gerbers, Excellon drill, assembly notes
Pin-to-pin netlist documentation written for someone who was not in the room
Power protection specified, not assumed — fusing, reverse polarity, TVS
for: An embedded product that needs a real board rather than a stack of dev kits
A prototype on perfboard that has to become something manufacturable
A team with firmware skills and no hardware engineer
Small-batch industrial products, 10 to 1,000 units
not_for: High-speed digital — DDR, multi-gigabit SERDES, RF front ends. Not our discipline and we will say so on the first call.
Boards needing more than four layers, usually
Safety-critical or certified medical hardware

offers.name: Firmware Rescue
offers.tagline: It half-works, and whoever wrote it is gone.
offers.summary: We take over an embedded codebase nobody understands any more and make it reliable: bring-up, fault detection, watchdogs, automatic recovery, and an update path so the next fix does not need a site visit.
offers.price_drivers: How reproducible the failure is and how much of the original build survives. A codebase that builds on one laptop costs less to rescue than one that builds nowhere.
deliverables: Reproducible build, documented, running on more than one machine
Fault detection and automatic recovery for the failures you actually see
Watchdogs, brownout handling and a defined behaviour for every reset cause
Offline tolerance — local commit first, sync second, no lost transactions
OTA update path so the next fix is a push, not a two-hour drive
A written map of the firmware for whoever comes after us
for: ESP32, STM32, RP2040, Arduino and PlatformIO codebases
Devices already deployed that are costing you support visits
A product that works until the network drops
Teams who inherited firmware with no author and no documentation
not_for: Ground-up firmware for a board that does not exist yet — that is Board-to-Fab
Linux or Android embedded systems. This is bare metal and RTOS.
Codebases we cannot build or hardware we cannot get hold of

offers.name: eFuelPro
offers.tagline: Every litre has a record, and the record has a receipt.
offers.summary: A forecourt terminal that reads the dispenser directly off the bus — not from a person typing numbers into a phone. Verifiable receipts, RFID loyalty and attendance, and a ledger that keeps working when the link drops.
offers.price_drivers: Number of pumps, and whether we already hold your dispenser's protocol. If we do not, a Protocol Decode Sprint comes first and is quoted separately.
deliverables: Epsilon1 terminal, installed and reading your dispenser directly
Self-calibrating decode — the device works out your pump's field map on site
Thermal receipts with a QR code that resolves to the online record
RFID loyalty per vehicle and per card, and staff attendance on the same reader
Offline-first ledger — sales never block on the network
Live dashboard: per-nozzle, per-shift, per-day, readable from anywhere
OTA configuration, including price per litre, with no site visit
for: Independent stations and small chains who cannot see what they sold until the shift ends
Dealers under a digital-monitoring obligation
Sites with old or mixed dispenser fleets that other integrators have turned down
OMCs wanting real telemetry rather than typed returns
not_for: Anyone who wants manual entry software — that market is well served and cheaper
Stations whose dispensers already expose a documented, supported integration
Single-pump sites where the monthly will not pay for itself

offers.name: Epsilon1
offers.tagline: A terminal that reads machines with undocumented protocols.
offers.summary: The board behind eFuelPro, pointed at any RS485 or Modbus machine. Generator, mill, chiller, weighbridge, loom — live readings into a ledger you can audit, on a terminal that keeps working when the network does not.
offers.price_drivers: Whether your machine class is one we have decoded before. If it is Modbus or otherwise documented, this is fast. If it is undocumented, a Protocol Decode Sprint comes first.
deliverables: Epsilon1 terminal — ESP32-S3, 4″ touch TFT, RS485, RFID, thermal printer, SD
Self-calibrating decode engine, so each site configures itself
Offline-first queue with idempotent event IDs
Cloud ledger and dashboard, or an API into yours
OTA configuration and firmware
Board files, libraries and firmware source under OEM terms
for: Flour mills, generators, cold storage, weighbridges, textile plant
Anyone running a fleet of machines they cannot see in real time
Integrators who want to build on a proven terminal rather than design one
not_for: Machines with a supported, documented API already — use it
Consumer or home automation
Anything needing certified safety instrumentation

offers.name: Device Penetration Test
offers.tagline: We take your device apart the way an attacker would.
offers.summary: Firmware extraction, debug-port discovery, bus interception, secrets in flash, update-path integrity. A hardware security assessment by people who design hardware — and a written report you can hand to a customer who asked whether your device is safe.
offers.price_drivers: How many distinct boards are in the product, whether the firmware is readable or locked, and whether you can give us a unit we are allowed to destroy. A device we can sacrifice is cheaper to assess than one we must return working.
deliverables: Written report: findings ranked by exploitability and impact, with reproduction steps
Firmware extraction attempt — SPI flash, JTAG/SWD, UART bootloader
Debug interface discovery: exposed UART, JTAG/SWD, test pads, unlocked fuses
Secrets audit — keys, credentials and tokens recoverable from the image
Bus interception on the device's own wires, including undocumented protocols
Update-path review: is an unsigned or downgraded image accepted?
Physical attack surface — enclosure, tamper evidence, exposed connectors
A remediation list written for the engineer who has to fix it, not for an auditor
for: You are shipping an embedded product and a customer has started asking security questions
IoT, industrial, metering, access-control or point-of-sale hardware
A device with a radio, a serial port, or a firmware update mechanism
You suspect the answer is bad and would rather find out before a customer does
not_for: Any device you do not own or have written authorisation from the owner to test. We ask for that authorisation in writing before we start, every time, and we will decline without it.
Web application or corporate network penetration testing — that is a different discipline and you want an accredited firm for it.
Certified assessments for PCI, SOC 2, FedRAMP or CE/UKCA sign-off. We are not an accredited lab and our report will not satisfy an auditor who needs one.
Formal cryptographic review or protocol proof work

offers.name: Authorisation Model Review
offers.tagline: Can tenant A read tenant B's row? We find out properly.
offers.summary: Multi-tenant isolation testing against your real schema and policies. Most testing proves you cannot log in as someone else. This proves that once you are legitimately logged in, you still cannot reach what is not yours.
offers.price_drivers: Number of roles, number of tables under policy, and whether there is a service-role key path that bypasses row-level security. Applications with one admin role are quick; ones with delegated per-organisation permissions are where the time goes.
deliverables: Per-table, per-role matrix of what is actually reachable, tested against a live instance
Cross-tenant read and write attempts from a legitimately authenticated session
Row-level security policy review against the schema, not against the documentation
Service-role and key-handling audit — anything that bypasses policy, and where it is exposed
Storage and file-access isolation, which is usually where it leaks
API and edge-function authorisation checks
Written findings with the failing query for each one, so a fix can be verified
for: Postgres and Supabase applications using row-level security
Any B2B product where two customers share a database
A team that inherited an application and does not know what its policies allow
You are about to sign an enterprise customer who will ask this question
not_for: Any system you do not own or have written authorisation from the owner to test. We ask in writing before we start and will decline without it.
Stacks other than Postgres. This offer is built on Postgres row-level security — MySQL, Mongo and DynamoDB tenancy models are a different problem and we do not cover them.
Testing against production data. Staging with representative data, always.
Full web application penetration testing — this is one deep slice, not broad coverage
Compliance certification

offers.name: Remote Protocol Decode
offers.tagline: You capture it. We decode it. Nobody gets on a plane.
offers.summary: The decode half of a Protocol Decode Sprint, without the site visit. We specify a capture rig, you run the stimulus matrix on your own machine, and we turn the resulting logs into a written specification and a working parser.
offers.price_drivers: How complete your captures are. A full stimulus matrix run to our instructions decodes quickly; a single log of idle traffic often cannot be decoded at all, and we will tell you that before you pay.
deliverables: A capture protocol: exactly what hardware to buy, where to clip it, what to vary and in what order
A free feasibility check on your first sample capture before you commit
Written protocol specification — framing, delimiters, field map, encoding, checksums
Validated parser in C/C++ or Python against your captures
Everything you need to re-derive it yourself
for: A machine anywhere in the world with somebody on site who can clip on a probe
Budgets that will not carry international travel
A first step before committing to the full on-site sprint
Anyone who has captures already and needs them read
not_for: Any equipment you do not own or have written authorisation from the owner to interface with. We ask for that authorisation in writing before we send the capture protocol, every time, and we will decline without it.
Encrypted or cryptographically authenticated protocols. We will not attempt to defeat an authentication scheme, and we would decline if asked.
Situations where nobody on site can safely attach a probe — take the full sprint instead

offers.name: BOM Risk Audit
offers.tagline: Find the part that goes end-of-life before your product does.
offers.summary: Send us your bill of materials. We come back with lifecycle status, real lead times, single-source exposure and a qualified alternate for every part that needs one.
offers.price_drivers: Line count, and how many parts need an alternate qualified rather than just looked up. Over 150 lines we quote per project.
deliverables: Lifecycle status for every line: active, NRND, or end-of-life
Real distributor stock and lead times, not catalogue availability
Single-source exposure flagged, with the risk stated plainly
A qualified alternate for every part that needs one, checked for footprint and spec compatibility
Cost roll-up at your build quantity
A ranked list of what to redesign around now rather than later
for: A board heading into its first production run
A product that has been in production a while and nobody has re-checked the BOM
Anyone who has been bitten by an allocation shortage once already
not_for: Schematic or layout review — that is Pre-Fab Design Review
Negotiating with distributors or placing orders on your behalf
BOMs with no part numbers. We need something to look up.

offers.summary: Send a datasheet, get back a KiCad symbol, footprint and 3D model built to the manufacturer's mechanical drawing and checked against IPC land pattern rules.
offers.price_drivers: Pin count and package complexity. A two-pin passive is at the floor; a BGA or a connector with a complex mechanical keepout is more.
deliverables: KiCad symbol with correct pin numbering, electrical types and naming
Footprint built to the manufacturer mechanical drawing, IPC-7351 land pattern
Courtyard and keepout, including antenna keepouts where the part needs one
3D model aligned to the footprint origin
A note of every assumption we had to make where the datasheet was ambiguous
for: An industrial module or connector with no decent library anywhere
Teams who have been burned by a downloaded footprint
Anyone standardising a house library they can actually trust
not_for: Parts with a good manufacturer-supplied KiCad library already — use it and save the money
Altium or Eagle native formats. We work in KiCad and export.
Footprint checking without the datasheet. We need the mechanical drawing.

Custom symbol and footprint libraries drawn from manufacturer datasheets
Orderable BOM with distributor part numbers and qualified alternates

Firmware reference: offline queue, RS485 framing and resynchronisation, OTA pattern
A licence that lets you modify it

Anyone building a vertical on an industrial edge device

Production-ready assembly. You still have to fabricate, assemble and test it.

Your customer list, exportable, owned by you

Dimensioned technical quotations generated as vector PDFs

offers.name: Ops Analyst
offers.tagline: Ask your database a question. Approve what it wants to change.
offers.summary: An AI analyst over your own operational data that answers in plain language — and can propose changes, but never make one without a human clicking approve. Scoped by the same permissions as the rest of your app.

Every answer grounded in a real query you can inspect
Proposed changes that require explicit human approval — never model discretion
Scoped by row-level security, so it sees only what the asking user may see
A full audit log of every question, query, proposal and approval
Streamed responses and prompt caching to keep it fast and cheap

Businesses that want AI over their data and refuse to hand it the keys
Postgres and Supabase applications with row-level security already in place

Customer-facing chatbots
Data you cannot legally process with a third-party model
